title: Schur bound for a measurable matrix integral kernel
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field]. Let $m\geq1$ and $p,q\geq0$ be integers, and let $G:\mathbf R^m\times\mathbf R^m\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C^p,\mathbf C^q)$ be Lebesgue measurable, with the Euclidean operator norm on matrices. Suppose $a,b\geq0$ are finite real numbers and $$\int\|G(x,y)\|\,dy\leq a\quad\text{for almost every }x,\qquad\int\|G(x,y)\|\,dx\leq b\quad\text{for almost every }y.$$ For each $h\in L^2(\mathbf R^m;\mathbf C^p)$, the integral $$Th(x)=\int G(x,y)h(y)\,dy$$ is absolutely convergent for almost every $x$ and determines an $L^2(\mathbf R^m;\mathbf C^q)$ class independent of representatives. It defines a bounded complex-linear map with $$\|Th\|_2\leq\sqrt{ab}\,\|h\|_2.$$ Here $L^2$ consists of measurable functions of finite squared-norm integral modulo almost-everywhere equality.

proof.text: Choose a measurable representative $h$ of the input class and put $k(x,y)=\|G(x,y)\|$, $v(y)=\|h(y)\|$ and $H(x,y)=G(x,y)h(y)$. Use Borel measure spaces with their Lebesgue measures; The completion clause of the parameter-measurability node gives almost everywhere measurable representatives of the Lebesgue-measurable functions for these Borel measures. The parameter-measurability node makes $G$, $h$ and the lifted map $(x,y)\mapsto h(y)$ almost everywhere strongly measurable. The finite-dimensional matrix space and $\mathbf C^p,\mathbf C^q$, regarded as real Banach spaces, are separable, also in dimension zero. Continuous operations on their simple approximations show that $k$, $v$, $H$ and $k(x,y)v(y)^2$ are almost everywhere measurable (and the vector map $H$ almost everywhere strongly measurable): apply the operation to the pair of simple approximations and pass to its pointwise limit outside their null sets. The same node gives almost everywhere strongly measurable sections of $H$ and of $G$. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbf R^m$ is sigma-finite, using the countable cover by bounded cubes.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Theorem 3.6, printed p.13 (PDF page 25). Agent-supplied analytic prerequisite; the source PDF could not be fetched online during this split.

proof.text: All integrals of nonnegative functions in this step are extended integrals, so no integrability is assumed in interchanging them. Set $U(x)=\int_y^- k(x,y)v(y)^2\,dy$. The Tonelli node gives its almost everywhere measurability and $$\int_x^-U(x)\,dx=\int_y^-v(y)^2\left(\int_x^-k(x,y)\,dx\right)dy\leq b\int_y v(y)^2\,dy=b\|h\|_2^2<\infty.$$ Extraction of the finite constant $v(y)^2$ in the inner integral and of $b$ in the outer integral, and the inequality from the almost-everywhere column bound, are the scalar and order clauses of that node. Its finiteness clause implies $U(x)<\infty$ almost everywhere. Intersect this full-measure set with the row-bound set and the section-measurability sets of step 1. On this intersection let $u(x)$ be the real value of $U(x)$, and set $u=0$ elsewhere. This is a nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable function and $\int u\leq b\|h\|_2^2$. The row integral $R(x)=\int k(x,y)\,dy$ is finite and at most $a$ there.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Theorem 3.6, printed p.13 (PDF page 25). Agent-supplied analytic prerequisite; the source PDF could not be fetched online during this split.

proof.text: For each $x$ in that full-measure set, the real functions $s_x(y)=\sqrt{k(x,y)}$ and $t_x(y)=\sqrt{k(x,y)}v(y)$ are measurable and square integrable, with $\|s_x\|_2^2=R(x)$ and $\|t_x\|_2^2=u(x)$. Apply the scalar clause of the existing real $L^2$ Cauchy–Schwarz node (fibre rank $1$): $$\int k(x,y)v(y)\,dy=\int|s_x(y)t_x(y)|\,dy\leq\sqrt{R(x)}\sqrt{u(x)}\leq\sqrt a\sqrt{u(x)}.$$ It also asserts integrability of this product. The identities $s_x^2=k$ and $t_x^2=kv^2$ use only $k,v\geq0$. This argument involves no division and includes $R(x)=0$ and $u(x)=0$.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Theorem 3.6, printed p.13 (PDF page 25). Agent-supplied analytic prerequisite; the source PDF could not be fetched online during this split.

proof.text: The definition of the operator norm gives $\|H(x,y)\|\leq k(x,y)v(y)$ pointwise. Apply the vector Bochner majorant node to the integrable majorant from step 3 and the almost everywhere strongly measurable section from step 1. Thus $\int_yH(x,y)\,dy$ is absolutely convergent for almost every $x$, and its norm is at most $\sqrt a\sqrt{u(x)}$. The parameter-integral node makes $J(x)=\int_yH(x,y)\,dy$, with zero for a nonintegrable section, almost everywhere strongly measurable. Its values on the exceptional null set do not affect its class. Squaring the estimate and using nonnegative integral monotonicity and constant extraction yields $$\int\|J(x)\|^2\,dx\leq a\int u(x)\,dx\leq ab\|h\|_2^2.$$ Hence $J$ defines the required $L^2$ output, and taking nonnegative square roots gives $\|J\|_2\leq\sqrt{ab}\,\|h\|_2$.

proof.text: If $h$ and $h'$ represent the same input class, choose a null set $N$ such that $h(y)=h'(y)$ off $N$. For every fixed $x$, the two integrands $G(x,y)h(y)$ and $G(x,y)h'(y)$ agree for every $y\notin N$. The almost-everywhere congruence clause of the Bochner node therefore identifies their integrals wherever the formula is used; in particular the two almost-everywhere defined outputs give the same $L^2$ class. Thus the construction descends to the quotient by almost-everywhere equality.

proof.text: For two inputs $h_1,h_2$ and $c\in\mathbf C$, intersect the full-measure sets on which the integrals for $h_1,h_2,h_1+h_2,ch_1$ are absolutely convergent. Matrix linearity gives $G(h_1+h_2)=Gh_1+Gh_2$ and $G(ch_1)=cGh_1$ pointwise; the Bochner additivity and scalar clauses give $T(h_1+h_2)=Th_1+Th_2$ and $T(ch_1)=cTh_1$ as classes. The estimate of step 4 gives boundedness of this complex-linear map. If $a=0$ or $b=0$ it forces the zero output class; no strict positivity was used. If $p=0$ or $q=0$, the relevant integrand is identically zero and the same formulas and all preceding bounds remain valid.
